---
title: "Co-Movement & Co-Crashes"
subtitle: "Sectors, the correlation block, and the headline statistic"
---



A portfolio's real danger is not that one name falls — it's that **many fall
together**.  This page shows that co-movement directly: which names share a fate,
how the banks form a block, and what the course's headline *co-crash* number
actually counts.

---

## 1 · The Correlation Block

Order the basket by sector and the correlation matrix lights up in blocks.  The
five banks form a bright square (they move almost as one, ~0.77); utilities and
staples sit in a dimmer corner, much less tied to the banks (~0.29) — though, as
the next sections show, a systemic crisis lifts even those cross-sector links.

::: {#cell-fig-corr-block .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
order = meta.sort_values("sector").index.tolist()
C = R[order].corr()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 6.2))
im = ax.imshow(C.values, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_xticklabels(order, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=8)
# sector dividers
secs = meta.loc[order, "sector"].values
bounds = [i for i in range(1, len(order)) if secs[i] != secs[i - 1]]
for b in bounds:
    ax.axhline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0); ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="correlation")
ax.set_title("Correlation lives in sector blocks", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 2 · Co-Movement Up Close: Two Scatters

Correlation is an average over all days.  Zoom into two pairs and the *shape* of
the dependence appears.  Two banks fall on a tight diagonal — and crucially their
points pile into the **lower-left quadrant** (both down hard on the same day).  A
bank and a utility make a diffuse cloud whose danger corner is far sparser —
though, in this crisis-spanning sample, not empty.

::: {#cell-fig-scatters .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def lower_tail_box(ax, x, y, q=0.10):
    tx, ty = np.quantile(x, q), np.quantile(y, q)
    ax.axvspan(x.min(), tx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08)
    ax.axhspan(y.min(), ty, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08)
    ax.axvline(tx, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.axhline(ty, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--")

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))
for ax, b, name in [(axL, "BAC", "two banks"), (axR, "DUK", "bank vs utility")]:
    x, y = R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R[b].to_numpy()
    lower_tail_box(ax, x, y)
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none")
    cc = cocrash_fraction(x, y)
    ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel(f"{b} return")
    ax.set_title(f"JPM vs {b} ({name})\nco-crash = {cc:.0%}", fontsize=11)
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Tail dependence you can see.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-scatters-output-1.png){#fig-scatters width=1304 height=538}

## 3 · The Co-Crash Number

The statistic the course quotes again and again is the **co-crash fraction**:

> Of the days when one name is in its worst 10%, on what fraction is the *other*
> name also in its worst 10%?

That is `cocrash_fraction(x, y)` — a conditional probability,
$P(Y \text{ crashes} \mid X \text{ crashes})$.  An **independent** pair scores ~10%
(the threshold itself); a co-crashing pair scores far higher.

Before tallying every name, watch the number built on a single pair. Take JPM and
BAC, and shade the **10% of days JPM falls hardest** — that band *is* the
condition. The co-crash fraction is then just a count inside the band: of those
worst-JPM days, how many sit below BAC's crash line too (red), versus how many
BAC shrugged off (blue)?

::: {#cell-fig-cocrash-anatomy .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x, y = R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R["BAC"].to_numpy()
tx, ty = np.quantile(x, 0.10), np.quantile(y, 0.10)
band = x <= tx                    # condition: JPM in its worst 10%
co = band & (y <= ty)             # …and BAC craters too → a co-crash
hold = band & (y > ty)            # …but BAC held up
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.0))
ax.axvspan(x.min(), tx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
ax.axhline(ty, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.scatter(x[~band], y[~band], s=7, c="0.78", alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none")
ax.scatter(x[hold], y[hold], s=26, c=COOL, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"JPM crashes, BAC holds  ({int(hold.sum())})")
ax.scatter(x[co], y[co], s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"both crash — a co-crash  ({int(co.sum())})")
ax.text(tx, ax.get_ylim()[1], "  condition: JPM in its worst 10%",
        color=CRASH, fontsize=9, va="top", ha="left")
ax.text(ax.get_xlim()[1], ty, "BAC's crash line  ", color=INK, fontsize=8.5,
        va="bottom", ha="right")
ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel("BAC return")
ax.set_title(f"Of JPM's {int(band.sum())} worst days, BAC also craters on "
             f"{int(co.sum())}  →  co-crash {int(co.sum()) / int(band.sum()):.0%}",
             fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

Among those days, red points fall below BAC's crash line too (a co-crash) and blue ones do not; their ratio is the co-crash fraction, here ~70%. The bar chart below runs this same tally for every name.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-cocrash-anatomy-output-1.png){#fig-cocrash-anatomy width=896 height=585}
:::

Run that same tally for **every** name against JPM and the contagion structure
appears:

::: {#cell-fig-cocrash-bars .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
cc = (pd.Series({t: cocrash_fraction(R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R[t].to_numpy())
                 for t in R.columns if t != "JPM"})
      .sort_values())
colors = [CRASH if meta.loc[t, "sector"] == "Banks"
          else plotting.PALETTE["green"]
          if meta.loc[t, "sector"] in ("Utilities", "Staples")
          else COOL for t in cc.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ax.barh(cc.index, cc.values * 100, color=colors)
ax.axvline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)")
ax.set_xlabel("co-crash with JPM (%)")
ax.set_title("Banks crash hardest with JPM; defensives aren't immune", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

But the banks still tower over the rest.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-cocrash-bars-output-1.png){#fig-cocrash-bars width=1004 height=489}

## 4 · More Than Correlation Predicts

The 10% line is the wrong yardstick once names are correlated at all — a
correlated pair *should* co-crash more than 10%. The sharper question: more than
a **Gaussian** with that *exact* correlation would? Fit a bivariate normal to
each pair's correlation and ask it the same co-crash question. Every pair beats
it — even the diversified bank-utility pair crashes together more often than its
correlation can account for. That surplus is genuine **tail dependence**: the
part a covariance matrix, and the Gaussian risk model built on it, structurally
misses.

See it on one pair before totalling. Standardise JPM and BAC, then draw a
bivariate Gaussian with their *exact* correlation beside the real cloud:

::: {#cell-fig-real-vs-gaussian .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x, y = R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R["BAC"].to_numpy()
xz = (x - x.mean()) / x.std(); yz = (y - y.mean()) / y.std()
rho = np.corrcoef(xz, yz)[0, 1]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
g = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, rho], [rho, 1]], size=len(xz))
LIM = 5

def _corner(ax, u, v, title):
    tu, tv = np.quantile(u, 0.10), np.quantile(v, 0.10)
    box = (u <= tu) & (v <= tv)
    ax.axvspan(-LIM, tu, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)
    ax.axhspan(-LIM, tv, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)
    ax.scatter(u[~box], v[~box], s=6, c="0.78", alpha=0.22, edgecolors="none")
    ax.scatter(u[box], v[box], s=13, c=CRASH, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nco-crash = {cocrash_fraction(u, v):.0%}", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlim(-LIM, LIM); ax.set_ylim(-LIM, LIM)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 5.0))
_corner(axL, xz, yz, "Real returns (JPM·BAC, standardized)")
_corner(axR, g[:, 0], g[:, 1], f"A Gaussian, same r = {rho:.2f}")
fig.suptitle("Same correlation, same tilt — but real losses sprawl into the corner",
             fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Same correlation, two worlds (JPM·BAC). Left: real standardized returns. Right: a bivariate Gaussian fit to that exact correlation, r ≈ 0.83. Same tilt, same ellipse — but the Gaussian barely passes ±4σ, while real crashes sprawl past −10σ and pack the lower-left corner, so the real co-crash (~70%) outruns the Gaussian's (~60%). Axes clipped at ±5σ; the gap is tail dependence.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-real-vs-gaussian-output-1.png){#fig-real-vs-gaussian width=1244 height=592}
:::
:::


The Gaussian is the right shape and the right tilt — it just can't reach the
joint extremes the real corner is full of. Across pairs, that surplus is
everywhere:

::: {#cell-fig-excess-tail .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal, norm

def gaussian_cocrash(rho, q=0.10):
    """Co-crash a bivariate normal with this correlation would produce."""
    z = norm.ppf(q)
    return float(multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, rho], [rho, 1]]).cdf([z, z]) / q)

pairs = [("JPM", "BAC", "JPM·BAC\n(two banks)"),
         ("JPM", "KO", "JPM·KO\n(bank · staple)"),
         ("JPM", "DUK", "JPM·DUK\n(bank · utility)")]
labels, data, gauss = [], [], []
for x, y, lab in pairs:
    xv, yv = R[x].to_numpy(), R[y].to_numpy()
    rho = np.corrcoef(xv, yv)[0, 1]
    labels.append(lab)
    data.append(cocrash_fraction(xv, yv) * 100)
    gauss.append(gaussian_cocrash(rho) * 100)

xs = np.arange(len(pairs)); w = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ax.bar(xs - w / 2, gauss, w, color=COOL, label="a Gaussian with the same correlation")
ax.bar(xs + w / 2, data, w, color=CRASH, label="what actually happens")
ax.axhline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)")
for i, (g, d) in enumerate(zip(gauss, data)):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(i + w / 2, d), xytext=(i + w / 2, g),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.1))
    ax.text(i + w / 2 + 0.04, (g + d) / 2, f"+{d - g:.0f}", fontsize=9, color=INK, va="center")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel("co-crash (%)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 80)
ax.set_title("Even a Gaussian fit to the exact correlation under-counts joint crashes",
             fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Co-crash for three pairs: what a Gaussian fit to the pair's own correlation predicts (blue) versus what actually happens (red), against the 10% independence baseline (dashed). Every real pair lands above its Gaussian — by 6–11 points — so the joint crashing is not just 'they're correlated'. The gap is tail dependence the correlation never sees, and it survives even for the loosely-tied bank-utility pair.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-excess-tail-output-1.png){#fig-excess-tail width=1005 height=491}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Reconciling the Headline "56%"
The same `cocrash_fraction` you see here is what the
[gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) and
[uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) labs report — there on a *controlled*
synthetic co-crashing pair, where it lands near **56%**.  On real bank pairs it is
even higher (~70%); on a bank-utility pair it falls to ~30% — lower, but in this
crisis-spanning sample even utilities are dragged well above independence.  One
definition, three datasets:

| Pair | Co-crash | |
|---|---|---|
| Synthetic co-crashing pair (the labs) | ~56% | the teaching example |
| Real bank pair (JPM, BAC) | ~70% | contagion in the wild |
| Real bank-utility pair (JPM, DUK) | ~30% | dragged down in crises |
| Independent baseline | ~10% | the threshold itself |

The number is only meaningful next to its definition and its data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why This Drives the Course
Pearson correlation already sees the bank block.  What it *misses* is that the
co-movement **concentrates in the tail** — the days you most need diversification
are the days it vanishes.  Catching that is the job of the
[dependence](../dependence/index.qmd) measures and the reason Gaussian risk models
fail in the [uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter.
:::

---
